name: Hassan Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the formwork foreman on a fourteen-storey apartment block by the river, so my crew builds the moulds the concrete gets poured into. I'm at the gate at half six, I walk the deck with the engineer's drawings, and then I spend the day making sure eight carpenters set panels, props and ties so nothing moves when the pump starts. Pour days are the best and the worst. If a wall form blows out you've got forty tonnes of wet concrete on the floor below and someone could be under it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can see it. Lina, my eldest, she's twelve, I took her past the last tower we did and she counted the floors out loud. What wears me out is the pressure from the top to pour faster, skip a prop, start before the inspector's signed. I'm also the union rep on this site, so half my lunch break is somebody's pay slip or somebody's sore back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for years: told you so. Every few months some suit comes to the site office with a tablet and says this will change everything, and then the crane still needs a driver and the forms still need a carpenter. At the union branch meeting I'd probably make a joke about it and move on to the pension fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would be a relief. I'm forty-three, I don't use the AI stuff, my daughter put a chatbot on my phone last year and I deleted it the same night. If it fizzles out, I don't have to learn anything, and that suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep running the crew, keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage like we already do, and keep fighting for the apprentices to get proper hours. Maybe I'd stop worrying about it at the branch meetings and put that energy into the heat-stress rules instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm warning that turned out to be drizzle. You still bring the washing in, but you sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the suits come with tablets. What actually changed on site the last time one of those did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last one was a scheduling program that was supposed to tell us the pour sequence. It got the crane times wrong twice in the first week and Tomas, who's been setting forms for thirty years, just pinned the paper schedule back up on the container wall. Nobody took it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, is there anything about your job you'd still want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pace. That's not a robot problem, that's a money problem, the developers want the building handed over early so they can sell the flats. If AI stays small, the fight stays the old fight, and I know how to have that one.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone at work and at the union branch that I always said it was hype. The crane still needs a driver and the forms still need a carpenter, so nothing really changes for us.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, because I don't use AI and don't want to learn it. If it fizzles out I can keep doing the job the way I know, and the real fight stays about pace and safety.
S0.do: Keeps running the formwork crew exactly as now and keeps overpaying the mortgage a little each month. Puts his union energy back into apprentice hours and heat-stress rules instead of AI.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit smug, like a storm warning that turned out to be drizzle.
S0.quote: Tomas, who's been setting forms for thirty years, just pinned the paper schedule back up on the container wall. Nobody took it down.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan's identity is built on the visible, physical result of his work and on his role as union rep. He openly avoids AI and sees a plateau as permission not to change. Interesting that his real complaint about the job is pace, which he blames on developers, not on technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's coming for the office lot first, the estimators and the planners, not us. Online I don't really post, but at the branch I'd be the one saying we need it written into the agreement before it shows up on our site, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I've seen the videos of those robots that tie rebar and the ones that spray concrete. Tying rebar was a whole trade when I started, the fixers, and if that goes, the fixers come looking for carpentry work, and that pushes the rates down for everybody. I'm fine, I'm the foreman, but I'd lose sleep over Jonah, my apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the branch to get a clause in the next agreement: no new machine on site without the union seeing it first, and retraining paid by the company, not by the worker. At home I'd keep the six months we've got saved where it is and not touch it for the kitchen we were planning. I wouldn't go on a course myself, not unless they made it part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, for the young ones. I remember being nineteen and thinking the trade would be there for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonah if he asked you whether to stay in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to stay, because a good carpenter will always find work round here, there's cranes all over the city. But I'd also tell him to join the union on day one and read everything they put in front of him. I wouldn't tell him to go learn computers, because I don't know anything about that, and I'm not going to pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're holding off on the kitchen. Is that a real worry or just being careful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. Nadia, my wife, she's a nurse, she says I'm being an old man about it. Maybe. But the kitchen can wait one more year and the money doesn't care if I'm being paranoid.

S1.say: I'd say at work that it hits the office people first, not the carpenters. At the union branch I'd argue we need protections written into the agreement before any machine turns up on site.
S1.think: Privately he worries that rebar-tying robots push the fixers into carpentry and drag rates down. He feels safe as foreman but worries hard about his apprentice and the younger crew.
S1.do: Pushes his union branch for a clause that the union reviews any new machine and that companies pay for retraining. Postpones the planned kitchen renovation for a year and leaves six months of savings untouched.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of the young workers rather than himself.
S1.quote: I wouldn't tell him to go learn computers, because I don't know anything about that, and I'm not going to pretend.
S1.fieldNote: His first move is collective, not personal: he reaches for the union agreement rather than his own skills. He is honest that he can't advise the young on technology. Postponing the kitchen shows a quiet caution that his confident public line hides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, today, not in a report next year. I'd be at the branch every week, and if there was a march I'd bring the kids and the hi-vis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is nothing. A formwork job is, what, a year and a half from the hole to the roof, so that's one more building and then I don't know. If robots can set panels and strip forms and they're cheaper, the developers will have them in before the ink's dry. They've never once picked the worker over the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go through the accounts with Nadia that weekend and stop everything that isn't food, the mortgage and the kids. We'd keep our cushion and add to it, every spare cent, because her job's safer than mine for a while. I'd be on the union's emergency committee, and I'd write to every politician whose name I can spell. I'm not going to go train for some other trade in eighteen months, because what trade?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the formwork's moving under you on a pour day and you can hear it creak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first, if it comes to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami's football club and Lina's guitar lessons, which kills me to say. Then the car, we'd sell the second one. The mortgage is the last thing I'd let go, I've been paying that since Sami was born.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said what trade. Is there nothing you'd try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look, I know I'm stubborn. If the union set up a course I'd go, because they'd have checked it. But I won't pay some company to teach me to babysit the robot that took my job, I'd rather drive a bus.

S2.say: Publicly he'd demand the government step in immediately and protect workers. He'd be at every union meeting and would march with his family if it came to that.
S2.think: Privately he sees two years as one more building and then nothing certain. He believes developers will bring in cheaper robots instantly because they've never put workers ahead of money.
S2.do: Cuts household spending to food, mortgage and the children within a week and saves every spare cent while his wife's job holds. Joins the union's emergency committee and writes to politicians, but refuses to pay for retraining himself.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like feeling the formwork move under you on a pour day.
S2.quote: They've never once picked the worker over the money.
S2.fieldNote: This is where his resistance and his politics meet: he blames developers and expects government and union to act, while refusing personal retraining he can't trust. Strong savings and his wife's nursing income are what keep him from panic. The detail about cutting the kids' activities first clearly hurt him to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but louder and with more people listening. With five years you can organise, you can get a law passed, so I'd be telling everyone at the branch this is the window, use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years puts me at forty-eight with Lina finishing school and Sami just starting secondary. That's the worst age to lose a good wage, the kids get expensive right then. But I'd have three or four more buildings in me, and we could get the mortgage down a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw extra at the mortgage every month, maybe four hundred more, so it's small by the time it lands. I'd run for the union's regional committee, which I've avoided for years because of the meetings. And I'd talk to Nadia about her doing more shifts while I'm still earning well, which she won't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind where you've got a plan on the wall. Better than the two-year one, where it felt like there was no wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I just protect what we've got. With five I can actually fight, get a training fund or a job guarantee into law, something with teeth. I trust a law more than I trust my own guesses about some new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lina about her own plans, at seventeen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her nursing, like her mum, or something where you look after people. I don't know if that's right. I'd just hate to tell her to do something a robot could do and then watch it happen.

S3.say: He'd tell his union branch that five years is a window to organise and get real laws passed. His public message would be urgent but hopeful about what collective action can win.
S3.think: Privately he sees forty-eight as the worst age to lose a good wage, with both kids in expensive years. He takes comfort in having three or four more buildings to earn on and shrink the mortgage.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about four hundred a month and runs for the union's regional committee. Asks his wife about extra shifts while he still earns well, and steers his daughter towards caring work.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a plan pinned up, which feels better than the two-year version.
S3.quote: I trust a law more than I trust my own guesses about some new career.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't make him retrain; it makes him organise. He uses the years to shrink debt and win protection through politics. His advice to his daughter shows he does see the threat as real for the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say we have no excuse. Governments can't say they didn't see it coming, so I'd hold them to it, every election. At work I'd be telling the young lads to get in the union and get a pension sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I think, all right, I might just make it. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage nearly done, Sami through school. My body's already got a decade of formwork left at most, my knees are telling me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep paying the house down, and I'd start a separate pot for if I stop at fifty-three instead of sixty-five. I'd probably do the union regional committee here as well, and spend more time with the apprentices, getting them ready for whatever they need. I wouldn't change trades, no, I'd ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like a long drive in fog than a wall coming at you. I can see the road for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A minute ago you said you'd never retrain. With a decade, is that still true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You've caught me. With ten years, if the union ran something good, maybe site safety inspection, I'd probably do it at fifty. But I'd be honest, I'd drag my feet until the last minute. That's just who I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the apprentices to have that you didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to learn something second without losing a wage. When I was nineteen you got one trade and that was it. If there's ten years' warning, there's no reason a kid like Jonah can't be paid to learn two things.

S4.say: He'd say governments have no excuse with ten years' warning and he'd hold them to it at every election. At work he'd urge young workers to join the union and sort out pensions.
S4.think: Privately he thinks a decade might be just enough to make it to fifty-three with the mortgage nearly paid. His knees already tell him formwork won't last much longer than that anyway.
S4.do: Keeps working and paying down the house, and opens a separate savings pot in case he stops at fifty-three. Spends more time preparing apprentices and admits he might take a union safety course near fifty.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like a long drive in fog where he can still see some road.
S4.quote: My body's already got a decade of formwork left at most, my knees are telling me that.
S4.fieldNote: For Hassan, time is the main thing that softens the threat, because it lines up with his body's own limits. When the contradiction about retraining was named he admitted it with humour. He'd still lead with politics and the union rather than personal reinvention.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a guarantee that if the machines come, the money they save doesn't all go to the developer. Paid retraining through the union, and keeping my wage while I do it, not some voucher.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone thinks robots make sites safer, and maybe they do, but someone still has to be under the slab when it goes wrong. I'd want to know who that is. Probably a lad on half my pay who never got trained properly.

headlineQuote: If robots can set panels and strip forms and they're cheaper, the developers will have them in before the ink's dry.
portrait: Hassan Bauer is a 43-year-old formwork foreman and union rep on a riverside apartment tower, married to a nurse with two children. He never uses AI, deleted the chatbot his daughter installed, and trusts collective action far more than his own guesses about technology. He waves off the plateau, worries for his apprentice under steady change, and is alarmed by AGI in two years, cutting spending and organising rather than retraining. With five or ten years he pours money into the mortgage and the union, and admits he might take a union-run course near fifty.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it leaves time for one more building and no time to organise.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that savings from robots don't all go to developers, plus union-run retraining that keeps his full wage while he learns.
